definitions.definition: U04 usage: the one reality realized as 'so'ham'; the soundless beyond nāda; the goal of renunciation; named as Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Rāma or the Goddess in the sectarian Upaniṣads.
U04 usage: the Self in the body-temple, identical with Brahman; threefold as outer, inner and supreme self in the Ātma Upaniṣad.

literal: resting-place of men / of the waters

definitions.definition: In the Vaiṣṇava and several yoga and renunciate Upaniṣads, the supreme Lord from whom Brahmā and Rudra arise, the Person in the solar orb, the one inner self.
In the Śaiva and yoga Upaniṣads the supreme Lord and the jīva's true nature: 'the jīva in the body is Śiva alone'; the jīva freed of the twenty faults is called Śiva.
Oṃ as analysed into measures and taught as the means of meditation, the renouncer's only study, the 'thread' and the tāraka; of three, four, twelve or sixteen measures.
The syllable Oṃ, explained in the Atharvaśiras as that which raises the breaths; its measures correspond to worlds, Vedas, fires and deities.
A measure of Oṃ: a, u, m and the half-measure; twelve measures in the Nādabindu, sixteen in the Nāradaparivrājaka.
The subtle fourth element of Oṃ beyond a, u and m; the 'head' of the Oṃ-bird.
The fourth state beyond waking, dream and deep sleep; placed between the brows (Triśikhi) or at the head.
(1) A fifth state beyond turīya, located at the brahmarandhra; (2) the name of the highest renouncer who lives like a cow, naked, the body as a corpse.
The witnessing consciousness into which, in samādhi, the world dissolves; the Self untouched by states.
The only true liberation, gained by knowledge alone (Muktikā); also the fruit of yoga in six months (Amṛtanāda).
Liberation while the body continues: the cessation of the mind's properties through destruction of vāsanā, dissolution of mind and knowledge of truth.
Liberation at the fall of the body when prārabdha is exhausted, like wind becoming still.
Residence in the Lord's world — first of the four kinds of liberation.
Nearness to the Lord — one of the four kinds of liberation.
Likeness of form with the Lord — one of the four kinds of liberation.
Union with the Lord — the highest of the four kinds of liberation; Śiva-sāyujya by the tripuṇḍra.
The mind, cause of bondage when attached to objects and of liberation when free of them; bound to prāṇa like a bird on a string.
Latent tendency that sustains mind; pure or impure; its destruction (vāsanā-kṣaya) with dissolution of mind and knowledge gives jīvanmukti.
Dissolution of mind, 'with form' in the jīvanmukta and 'without form' in the videhamukta.
The movement of prāṇa, one of the two seeds of the mind-tree.
The state in which the mind has dissolved; 'unmanībhāva'; beyond merit and sin.

equivalents.note: Both name the mind-less state; amanaska is the later part of tāraka-yoga, unmanī the state reached by nāda.

definitions.definition: The end of sound and of mind; the goal of nāda-yoga; also a measure of the sixteen-measured praṇava.
The later (uttara) tāraka, in which the mind is like an udder after milking.
(1) The light between the brows and the yoga of targets that carries across saṃsāra; (2) the mantra Rudra gives the dying at Avimukta (Oṃ, the Rāma mantra or the Nārāyaṇa mantra).
Object of attention in tāraka-yoga: inner, outer or intermediate.
One of the five spaces seen in the intermediate target (ākāśa, parākāśa, mahākāśa, sūryākāśa, paramākāśa).
A stage of knowledge (seven) or of ignorance (seven); also the four stages of yoga.
First stage of knowledge: the wish for liberation.
Second stage of knowledge: inquiry with scripture and the wise.
Third stage: the mind made subtle.
Fourth stage: resting in the Self; the knower of Brahman.
Fifth stage: non-attachment; the excellent knower.
Sixth stage: objects no longer appear.
Seventh stage: no difference; one's own nature.
Karma that has begun to bear fruit; for the knower it moves the body but does not bind; its exhaustion brings bodiless liberation.
The unstruck inner sound, heard in stages, in which the mind dissolves; 'no mantra higher than nāda'.
The point of Oṃ; the seed-essence (white and red) whose retention the haṭha passages seek; identified with mind.
A subtle stage of the praṇava after nāda and bindu; a light seen in the west.
The unstruck sound heard within; also the heart centre.
Holding attention on the inner sound; it destroys vāsanās.
The self moving with the breath (ha out, sa in), meditated as a bird and repeated naturally 21,600 times a day; also the third kind of renouncer.

equivalents.note: Haṃsa reversed is so'ham ('I am He'): the same breath-mantra read as identity.

definitions.definition: The identity-formula into which the haṃsa is reversed; the renouncer's worship and meditation.
The mantra 'recited' by the breath without effort (ajapā-gāyatrī).
The first, unmanifest level of speech, where it 'sprouts'.
The second level of speech, where it puts forth two leaves.
The third level of speech, in the heart, where it buds.
Spoken speech coming forth through the palate.
U04 usage: the four sayings given as secret teaching (Śukarahasya) and at renunciation; read as the Goddess in the Bahvṛca.
Channel of breath; 72,000 arise from the kanda; ten or fourteen are principal.
The central channel, path of liberation, 'devourer of time', the supreme tīrtha.
The left channel, carrying the moon.
The right channel, carrying the sun.
The bulb near the navel from which the channels spread.
A centre of the subtle body; six (or nine) in the Yoga Upaniṣads; also the Śrīcakra.
A support-point of attention in the body (sixteen in the Yogacūḍāmaṇi); the base centre.
The base centre at the anus, with the triangle where kuṇḍalinī lies.
The centre at the genitals.
The navel centre, a twelve-spoked wheel where the jīva wanders.
The throat centre.
The centre in the head, between the brows.
The thousand-petalled lotus above the centres where Śakti unites with Śiva.
The opening at the crown; seat of the state beyond the fourth; exit of the breath that does not return.
One of three knots (of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra) pierced by kuṇḍalinī.
The coiled power at the base that blocks the door of Brahman and, awakened, rises to Śiva.
The vital breath; the self in the Brahma Upaniṣad; chief of the ten vāyus; its vibration is a seed of mind.
The downward breath, seated at the anus.
The breath at the navel, distributing food.
The breath in the throat.
The breath pervading the body.
One of eighteen vital points through which breath and attention are moved in pratyāhāra; 'cut' in the Kṣurikā.
Four seats in the body — Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, Uḍyāna.
The body ripened by the fire of yoga (opposite apakva).
Ten restraints (non-injury … purity), each with an outer and an inner meaning; moderate diet is chief.
Ten observances (austerity … vows); non-injury is called chief of the niyamas in the Yogatattva.
Posture — four, eight, nine, eleven or seventeen named; inwardly, indifference or the seat where Brahman-thought flows.
Regulation of breath; inwardly, seeing all as Brahman (exhalation negating the world, inhalation 'I am Brahman', retention steadiness).
Retention of breath; sahita (with inhalation and exhalation) or kevala (spontaneous). Methods recorded summary-only.
Spontaneous suspension of breath; its signs and the awakening of kuṇḍalinī. Summary only.
Exhalation; inwardly, negation of the world or renunciation of objects.
Inhalation; inwardly, 'I am Brahman' or scriptural knowledge.
Withdrawal of the senses; five kinds, including seeing all as the Self.
Concentration; the five element-concentrations; holding mind in the Self.
Meditation with or without qualities; 'so'ham'; one-pointedness on consciousness.
In the Yoga Upaniṣads: the union of jīvātman and paramātman; the forgetting of meditation; distinguished from deep sleep; for the Mahāvākya, realization is not mere samādhi.
In the Amṛtanāda's six limbs, reasoning not opposed to the āgamas.
Moderate, sweet, unctuous food leaving a quarter of the stomach empty; chief of the yamas.
A seal of body, gaze or attention (mahāmudrā, khecarī, śāmbhavī, vaiṣṇavī, ṣaṇmukhī); also the renouncer's inner 'seal'.
The three locks — root, abdominal, throat.
A secret seal learned from a guru with its mantra; bodily procedures recorded summary-only; inwardly the gaze or the renouncer's seal.
The seal of the open, unblinking gaze with attention on the inner target.
Leading kuṇḍalinī upward; summary only.
Dissolution of mind; laya-yoga meditates on the Lord in all activity; 'laya is lord of the breath'; also an obstacle in samādhi (torpor).
Haṭha-yoga: eight limbs with mudrās; in the Yogaśikhā, the union of ha (sun) and ṭha (moon).
The fourth of the four yogas; in the Yogaśikhā the union of rajas and retas.
The first of the four yogas; repetition, or the natural haṃsa reversed.
First of the four stages of yoga.
Second stage, in which breaths, mind and selves unite.
Third stage, in which kuṇḍalinī enters the suṣumnā.
Fourth stage: natural yoga; liberation while living.
A power arising from practice; contrived or spontaneous; an obstacle to hide, or the test of a siddha.
Concentration on an object yielding a power (Śāṇḍilya).
Omen foretelling death.
Renunciation of household and rites for the wandering life; truly, the union of jīva and Self.
One who has renounced; of four or six kinds.
The wandering ascetic; one night in a village, five in a town, the rains in one place.

equivalents.note: Parivrājaka stresses wandering, saṃnyāsin the act of renunciation; the texts use both for the fourth āśrama.

definitions.definition: The renouncer-ascetic; the texts address him as yati.
One who lives on alms; four kinds in the Bhikṣuka Upaniṣad.
First kind of renouncer: keeps topknot, thread, staff and water-pot; eats in one place.
Second kind: triple staff, ochre, eight mouthfuls from many houses.
Third kind: one night in a village, five in a town; lunar fasts.
Fourth kind: no topknot or thread; knowledge as staff; beyond dharma and adharma; attains the world of truth or liberation.
The renouncer who has shaken off saṃsāra, beyond castes and stages, without marks or rules; etymologized syllable by syllable.
Renouncer with a single staff; truly, 'one who bears the staff of knowledge'.
Renouncer with the triple staff (Vaiṣṇava mark); inwardly, restraint of speech, body and mind.
The renouncer's staff, of bamboo; never to be left more than three arrow-shots away (Sannyāsa); or the staff of knowledge.
The renouncer's water-pot, among the permitted articles.
The loincloth kept by most kinds of renouncer, or abandoned by the highest.
The discoloured or ochre cloth of the renouncer.
The tuft of hair; abandoned by the paramahaṃsa (knowledge is his topknot) or kept for life by the Vaiṣṇava renouncer.
The sacrificial thread; for the renouncer the Self, Brahman or praṇava is the true thread.
The renunciation declaration ('I have renounced'; 'I have risen above the desires for wife, wealth and worlds').
Purificatory oblation in the renunciation rite.
The renouncer's own funerary offering, among the eight śrāddhas.
The renouncer's gift: 'fearlessness to all beings from me'.
The three desires — for wife/sons, wealth and worlds — risen above in renunciation.
Alms gathered a little from many houses, after the cooking fires are out.
Food begged by the renouncer; five kinds; better than unsolicited food.
Renunciation in mortal danger, by mind and speech.
Renunciation after passing through the stages.
Renunciation by one who has realized.
Renunciation in order to realize, keeping the insignia.
The knower beyond castes and stages of life.
The liberated renouncer's freedom from rule.
Dispassion, the condition of renunciation ('the very day one becomes dispassionate'); the oil of the lamp of knowledge (Dakṣiṇāmūrti).
Discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues and longing for liberation.
Sacred ash, prepared with mantras; worn in the pāśupata vow and the tripuṇḍra.
One of the five names of sacred ash.
Three horizontal lines of ash, each with its correspondences.
Bead from Kālāgnirudra's tears, worn with mantras.
Rosary into whose beads the fifty letters a–kṣa are invoked.
The jīva bound by ego and the bonds.
The bond of the paśu, loosened by the pāśupata vow.
The Lord of beings, all-knowing, doer of the five acts; witness who empowers the senses.
Smearing ash with 'fire is ash …' for release from bonds.
Kāśī, where Rudra gives the tāraka to the dying; located in the body between brows and nose.
The Yajurveda's Rudra litany, whose recitation gives immortality.
Vaiṣṇava vertical mark of gopīcandana.
White clay from Dvārakā for Vaiṣṇava marks.
The yantra of Tripurā; the body contemplated as it.
One of the fifteen lunar goddesses of Tripurā.
The fourfold form of the Lord (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) in the Triśikhi's concentrations and the Mudgala.
The Lord's transcendent three quarters beyond māyā.
Offering food to the five breaths as an inner agnihotra.
Crossing the Kali age by the sixteen names.
